title: nanomedicine: reshaping clinical practice
display_name: Nanomedicine: reshaping clinical practice
abstract: " for i was never so small as this before, never!" lewis carroll, alice's adventures in wonderland (1865) the 6th key symposium on nanomedicine was held in stockholm, sweden on september 9 11, 2009. the symposium featured presentations from numerous leading scientists in the field and was divided into four sessions, reflecting some of the principal areas of research in nanomedicine, i.e., regenerative medicine, drug delivery, imaging and diagnostics, and finally, toxicology and risk assessment. this review aims to convey the excitement that was evident at this event and also to summarize some of the key messages. in addition, in the current volume of the journal of internal medicine, several of the speakers at the symposium have provided state-of-the-art reviews of specific areas of research on the application of nanotechnologies in medicine (nanomedicine) and/or on potential adverse effects of engineered nanomaterials (nanotoxicology). there has been considerable progress in recent years in the field of regenerative medicine due to the emergence of nanotechnology and specifically as a result of the use of nano-textured surfaces or topographies to facilitate biomimetic tissue engineering. in his keynote lecture, dr. teruo okano (tokyo woman's medical university) discussed a method of 'cell sheet engineering' for scaffoldless tissue engineering, based on an innovative polymer-based technology, and its potential application in a variety of clinical conditions. using temperature-responsive culture surfaces of poly(n-isopropylacrylamide), cells can be harvested as a contiguous sheet of cells with an intact extracellular matrix and thick tissues are constructed by layering of these cell sheets in an iterative process [1]. transplantation of such cell sheets onto damaged hearts improved heart function in animal models, and evidence was also presented for beneficial clinical outcome in a patient suffering from dilated cardiomyopathy. in addition, dr. okano reported that clinical trials have been initiated for the assessment of cell sheet engineering of ocular cell sheets for the improvement of visual acuity of patients with corneal stem cell deficiencies. dr. cato laurencin (university of connecticut) discussed recent advances in the fabrication of nanostructured scaffolds from polymeric and composite materials for musculoskeletal tissue regeneration. these important studies are beginning to unravel how molecular cues that occur as nanoscale structures interact with cells and open up opportunities to modulate such cues to improve the regeneration of damaged tissue. nanofibers mimicking the structure of natural extracellular matrix are generated by a process of electrospinning of polymers, and elegant studies in which this technology was applied to the repair of tendons and the generation of bone were presented. in addition, 3d porous scaffolds have been shown to support the growth of genetically engineered stromal cells for sustained release of endothelial growth factors that promote vascularization [2]. in a similar vein, dr. j ns hilborn (uppsala university) presented promising preclinical studies on a new hyaluronan-based carrier for the osteoinductive growth factor, bone morphogenetic protein-2 (bmp-2), that has been shown to function as an injectable replacement for bone grafts in animal experiments. dr. samuel stupp (northwestern university) presented recent work on the development of a broad class of amphiphilic molecules that are programmed to self-assemble into nanoscale filaments with the capacity to display signals to cells and bind specific proteins or dna [3]. these nanostructures have been developed for a number of biological targets and clinical conditions, including repair and regeneration of neurons, angiogenesis, as well as bone and cartilage regeneration. in a recently published preclinical study, remarkable efficiency in functional recovery after spinal cord injury was demonstrated. treatment with peptide amphiphile (pa) molecules that self-assemble in vivo into supramolecular nanofibers resulted in the regeneration of both descending motor fibres and ascending sensory fibres through the lesion site in a clip compression model of spinal cord injury in mice. treatment with the pa also resulted in significant behavioural improvement. dr. joakim spatz (max-planck-institute for metals research) explored the concept of artificial engineering of cellular responses based on the use of an inorganic or polymeric support, patterned with specific signalling molecules in well-defined nanoscopic geometries. examples of environmental sensing resulting from the crosstalk between the assembly of dynamic actin-integrin links known as focal adhesions and the forces that come into play in the associated cytoskeletal network owing to actin polymerization and actomyosin contraction were presented. a deeper understanding of how cells sense their environment could suggest new strategies in tissue engineering and regenerative medicine. the application of nanotechnology to drug delivery is expected to have considerable impact on the pharmaceutical and biotechnological industries. the first lecture in the session on drug delivery was delivered by dr. robert langer (massachusetts institute of technology) who presented early work on tumour angiogenesis and the application of the so-called rabbit corneal pocket assay for monitoring of neovascular growth in live animals. the latter assay was instrumental for the discovery and purification of angiogenesis-regulatory molecules. he then focused on the issue of gene therapy and prefaced this discussion by citing the words of dr. inder verma, a leading authority on the development of viruses as gene therapy vectors, who famously said that 'there are only three problems in gene therapy: delivery, delivery, and delivery'. viral vectors are efficient but they pose safety concerns. synthetic vectors are potentially safer, cheaper and easier to produce, yet they are currently less efficient. however, recent studies have shown that lipid-like materials designated as 'lipidoids' that have been identified by high-throughput screening approaches outperform other commonly used transfection reagents and thus show promise for delivery of rna interference (rnai) therapeutics [4]. dr. gabriel lopez-berestein (university of texas md anderson cancer centre) discussed exciting new developments in sirna technology for cancer therapy [5]. one of the main challenges is to develop safe and effective carriers for systemic administration of sirnas, and dr. lopez-berestein described recent studies focusing on cationic liposomes as nanocarriers of sirna. promising results from animal models of ovarian cancer were presented. it was also noted that the expression of dicer and drosha, components of the cellular rna interference machinery, varies in specimens of ovarian cancer in patients, and, moreover, that the levels of dicer and drosha mrna in ovarian cancer cells have associations with outcomes. these observations highlight the need for 'personalized medicine' and this was indeed one of the common themes of this symposium. in a sense, the era of nanomedicine can be viewed as the era of personalized medicine [6]. multi-functional nanocarriers for combined therapeutic and diagnostic purposes are currently being developed in research laboratories (fig. 1). dr. naomi halas (rice university) explored the opportunities for cancer treatment without the use of a conventional, pharmaceutical drug. in this paradigm, nanosized gold shells (hollow or core-shell structures) serve as light-scattering beacons and impart highly effective therapeutic responses via their unparalleled light-to-heat conversion properties. the latter effect has been employed to induce cell death and tumour regression in various animal models, and the same concept is now being evaluated in clinical trials [7]. importantly, this nanoparticle platform for thermal ablation of tumours can be combined with magnetic resonance imaging (mri) contrast agents for the enhancement of simultaneous imaging modalities. multi-functional nanoparticles for drug delivery. schematic of a multi-functional nanocarrier that combines a specific targeting agent (usually an antibody or peptide) with nanoparticles for imaging (such as semiconductor nanoparticles/quantum dots or magnetic nanoparticles), a cell-penetrating agent, a stimulus-sensitive element for drug release, a stabilizing polymer to ensure biocompatibility (commonly polyethylene glycol) and the therapeutic compound(s) of interest. reprinted from [18] with permission from elsevier. dr. ruth duncan (cardiff university), one of the pioneers in research on polymer therapeutics, addressed the question as to where we are on the road to clinical application of nanomedicine. there is growing optimism that ever more sophisticated polymer-based vectors will be a significant addition to the armamentarium currently used for cancer therapy [8]. however, future success will depend on the choice of an appropriate (nontoxic) polymer in relation to its proposed use and route of administration, the rational design of new drugs and drug carriers, and improved analytical techniques for measuring polymer characteristics. in addition, an improved, quantitative understanding of pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics is also needed to bridge the gap between the bench and the clinic. there has been an increasing interest in ordered mesoporous silica matrices for biomedical applications. indeed, the combination of properties of these mesoporous materials such as high surface areas, and their textural properties, especially the well-ordered pore geometries, make these materials attractive for a variety of applications. dr. maria vallet-regi (the complutense university of madrid) provided exciting glimpses of recent studies on nanostructured mesoporous silica for regeneration of bone tissue and as drug delivery systems [9]. dr. alexander kabanov (university of nebraska) discussed polymeric micelles structures self-assembled from amphiphilic block copolymers containing hydrophilic and hydrophobic components. such structures form nanosized (10 100 nm) core-shell structures. drug molecules can be incorporated into the cores of the micelles and polymeric micellar drug formulations are currently undergoing clinical trials for treatment of cancer and other diseases. dr. kabanov presented remarkable results on such micelles with 'phenotypic selectivity' in which micelles loaded with cytotoxic drug are toxic to cancer cells and sensitize multi-drug resistant tumour cells, whilst sparing normal cells that do not internalize the micelles because of differences in their endocytic machineries. phase iii clinical trials of such block copolymers for treatment of oesophageal cancer are in progress. dr. vladimir torchilin (northeastern university) focused on the application of nanocarriers for delivery of 'undeliverable' drugs, i.e. drugs with poor solubility, low stability and rapid clearance from systemic circulation. more than half of all drug candidates are abandoned due to poor solubility and hence cannot be delivered as therapeutics. however, by applying layer-by-layer technology (alternate coating of nanoparticles of poorly soluble drugs with layers of oppositely charged biocompatible soluble polymers), stable nanocolloidal formulations of drugs can be prepared. dr. torchilin illustrated this concept with data on the preparation of paclitaxel-loaded 'immuno-micelles' bearing anti-tumour antibodies which were shown to accumulate in vivo in a lung carcinoma model in mice resulting in efficient inhibition of tumour growth [10]. the ability to measure and visualize proteins and their patterns of interactions and modifications is of key importance in basic science and in medicine, as this can afford new insights into cellular processes and their perturbation in disease. in his lecture, dr. ulf landegren (uppsala university) delved into the cellular proteome and presented a technology known as proximity ligation assay (pla) that harnesses dna for construction of protein assays of considerable specificity and sensitivity. examples of pla-based detection of disease markers and of viral proteins were given, including results from a recently published study on the detection of avian influenza virus, demonstrating that pla is nearly as sensitive as a commonly used real-time pcr assay, and much more sensitive than a conventional sandwich elisa, utilizing the same antibody. dr. charles lieber (harvard university) presented a visionary lecture on nanowire electronic devices and their potential application for ultrasensitive, multiplexed, label-free detection of disease markers [11]. importantly, because the sizes of biological macromolecules are comparable to nanowire building blocks, these structures represent natural transducers for detection in the size-range of biological systems. dr. lieber reported on the feasibility of detection of cancer markers at femtomolar concentrations in biological samples using silicon-nanowire field-effect devices. in addition, more recent studies have demonstrated that nanowire transistor arrays can be interfaced with specific regions of acute brain slices of the olfactory bulb to detect localized neuronal activities with very high resolution, and that these devices can also be employed to record electrical activity in embryonic chicken cardiomyocytes with high sensitivity. together, these studies suggest that research at the interface between engineered nanosystems and endogenous biosystems may yield important advances in diagnostics and clinical medicine. dr. sunney xie (harvard university) presented fascinating data on new imaging techniques for the visualization of biochemical processes. imaging of single fluorescent proteins with millisecond time resolution and nanometer spatial precision have thus been developed. such technologies may yield insights into the mechanisms of many processes in molecular biology, such as dna protein interactions, gene regulation, transcription, translation and replication. in addition, sensitive, label-free imaging techniques based on stimulated raman scattering microscopy for small drugs or metabolites [12], and stimulated emission microscopy for chromophores such as hemeproteins with undetectable fluorescence were discussed. these imaging modalities offer exciting possibilities for biomedicine. dr. hjalmar brismar (royal institute of technology) discussed techniques for studies of protein mobility using quantum dot-based single particle tracking. quantum dots (inorganic semiconductor nanocrystals) are well-suited for single particle tracking as they are photostable, thus permitting long exposure times/time-lapse recordings under the microscope. dr. chad mirkin (northwestern university) discussed polyvalent nucleic acid nano-conjugates and explored how these constructs can be utilized in biodiagnostics and for regulation of gene expression. it was noted that the application of dna nanoparticle (e.g. gold nanoparticle) conjugates in biodetection has the potential to challenge the medical community to move diagnostic tests from centralized laboratories to the point-of-care as these novel and sensitive methods allow for miniaturization of the test platform; indeed, us food and drug administration (fda)-approved tests are available for the in vitro diagnosis of several diseases including cystic fibrosis and blood coagulation disorders. one of the most significant obstacles for systemic delivery of payloads (drugs, nucleic acids) using nanocarriers is the foreign particle clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system. the rate and extent of removal is determined by the physico-chemical properties of the materials used. dr. martin philbert (university of michigan) discussed strategies for evasion of macrophage clearance by the use of degradable polyacrylamide-based hydrogels. to avoid the accumulation of polyacrylamide-based nanoparticles in the body, short chain polyacrylamides were assembled into nanoparticles with degradable cross-linkers. these payloads are stable in aqueous environments but they quickly disintegrate under cytoplasmic conditions so as to release drugs once they enter cells. the development of biodegradable polymers may significantly reduce the toxicity of the nanocarrier. sustainable development of the nanotechnologies for use in the clinic will necessitate close attention to safety issues [13]. dr. g nter oberd rster (university of rochester) outlined basic concepts guiding nanotoxicological research, including the significance of dose, and the importance of a thorough understanding of physico-chemical properties of nanoparticles [14]. dr. oberd rster also presented recent data from animal studies of gold nanoparticles of different sizes in which the importance of the route of administration (intravenous injection versus inhalation) and the influence of particle coating/surface modification for biodistribution of particles were assessed. numerous challenges remain in nanotoxicological research: assessment of human and environmental exposure, identification of potential hazards of engineered nanomaterials, and the issue of biopersistence in tissues all need to be taken into account to perform meaningful risk assessment. the question as to whether nanoparticles can cross biological barriers and accumulate in secondary target organs following, for instance, inhalation has been debated in recent years. dr. wolfgang kreyling (german research centre for environmental health) presented interesting quantitative data on the accumulation of small fractions of nanoparticles (iridium, carbon, gold, titanium dioxide) in all secondary organs studied including the brain, heart and even in foetuses. the fractions were generally low but this depended strongly on particle size and surface modifications of the particles and on the route of administration. dr. kreyling concluded that it is possible that chronic exposure to nanoparticles may lead to accumulation in secondary organs at levels that are sufficient to induce adverse health effects. however, long-term exposure studies have yet to be conducted. dr. anna shvedova (national institute for occupational safety and health) focused her presentation on studies of single-walled carbon nanotubes (swcnt), which are common in a wide range of different technological applications and are also being considered for biomedical applications, including as vectors for delivery of drugs or nucleic acids. recent in vivo studies have shown that swcnt can elicit strong inflammatory and early-onset fibrogenic responses coupled with the induction of oxidative stress in the lung of mice exposed via pharyngeal aspiration or inhalation [15]. these effects occurred at doses of potential relevance to occupational scenarios. considerable attention has been drawn to the potential similarities between carbon nanotubes and asbestos fibres. dr. shvedova reported that inhalation of swcnt resulted in the occurrence of mutations in the k-ras oncogene in mice. moreover, in vitro studies conducted in primary human bronchial epithelial cells demonstrated that swcnt cause frequent disruption of cell division due to interference with the mitotic spindle. however, long-term studies are needed to assess whether these alterations will result in the formation of tumours of the lung or mesothelium. swcnt are considered to be highly biopersistent and are not readily recognized or engulfed by macrophages in the absence of specific surface modifications of these materials. dr. valerian kagan (university of pittsburgh) presented exciting data on the enzymatic biodegradation in vitro of swcnt in human neutrophils, key players of the innate immune system. biodegradation was accomplished through enzymatic catalysis by human neutrophil-derived myeloperoxidase (hmpo). functionalization of swcnt with immunoglobulin (igg) promoted cellular internalization of swcnt and enhanced the hmpo-dependent biodegradation. importantly, using an established model of pharyngeal aspiration of swcnt, it was shown that biodegradation of swcnt in vitro nullified their propensity to induce pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis. these findings indicate that biomedical applications of cnts may be achievable under conditions of carefully controlled biodegradation. when nanoparticles are introduced into the body, intentionally or unintentionally, what do cells really see? dr. kenneth dawson (university college dublin) discussed this important aspect of nanomedicine/nanotoxicology, and introduced the concept of a protein 'corona' that results from a dynamic exchange of proteins and lipids between the surface of nanoparticles and environment [16]. the exchange rates are sometimes so slow that many biological responses are likely defined by these associated biomolecules. it follows from this argument that it is of crucial importance to develop methods to study the identity of title: camelid single-domain antibodies: historical perspective and future outlook
display_name: Camelid Single-Domain Antibodies: Historical Perspective and Future Outlook
abstract: tremendous effort has been expended over the past two and a half decades to understand many aspects of camelid heavy chain antibodies, from their biology, evolution, and immunogenetics to their potential applications in various fields of research and medicine. in this article, i present a historical perspective on the development of camelid single-domain antibodies (sdabs or v h hs, also widely known as nanobodies) since their discovery and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of these unique molecules in various areas of research, industry, and medicine. commercialization of camelid sdabs exploded in 2001 with a flurry of patents issued to the vrije universiteit brussel (vub) and later taken on by the vlaams interuniversitair instituut voor biotechnologie (vib) and, after 2002, the vib-founded spin-off company, ablynx. while entrepreneurial spirit has certainly catalyzed the exploration of nanobodies as marketable products, ip restrictions may be partially responsible for the relatively long time span between the discovery of these biomolecules and their entry into the pharmaceutical market. it is now anticipated that the first v h h-based antibody drug, caplacizumab, a bivalent anti-vwf antibody for treating rare blood clotting disorders, may be approved and commercialized in 2018 or shortly thereafter. this elusive first approval, along with the expiry of key patents, may substantially alter the scientific and biomedical landscape surrounding camelid sdabs and pave the way for their emergence as mainstream biotherapeutics.

title: comparative performance of an elitist teaching-learning-based optimization algorithm for solving unconstrained optimization problems
display_name: Comparative performance of an elitist teaching-learning-based optimization algorithm for solving unconstrained optimization problems

authorships.name: R. Venkata Rao
institutions: Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology Surat

authorships.name: Vivek Patel
institutions: Sardar Vallabhbhai National Institute of Technology Surat

abstract: teaching-learning-based optimization (tlbo) is a recently proposed population based algorithm, which simulates the teaching-learning process of the class room.this algorithm requires only the common control parameters and does not require any algorithm-specific control parameters.in this paper, the effect of elitism on the performance of the tlbo algorithm is investigated while solving unconstrained benchmark problems.the effects of common control parameters such as the population size and the number of generations on the performance of the algorithm are also investigated.the proposed algorithm is tested on 76 unconstrained benchmark functions with different characteristics and the performance of the algorithm is compared with that of other well known optimization algorithms.a statistical test is also performed to investigate the results obtained using different algorithms.the results have proved the effectiveness of the proposed elitist tlbo algorithm.

title: international con sensus on drug allergy
display_name: International<scp>Con</scp>sensus on drug allergy

authorships.name: David A. Khan
institutions: The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center

abstract: abstract when drug reactions resembling allergy occur, they are called drug hypersensitivity reactions ( dhr s) before showing the evidence of either drug specific antibodies or t cells. dhr s may be allergic or nonallergic in nature, with drug allergies being immunologically mediated dhr s. these reactions are typically unpredictable. they can be life threatening, may require or prolong hospitalization, and may necessitate changes in subsequent therapy. both underdiagnosis (due to under reporting) and overdiagnosis (due to an overuse of the term allergy ) are common. a definitive diagnosis of such reactions is required in order to institute adequate treatment options and proper preventive measures. misclassification based solely on the dhr history without further testing may affect treatment options, result in adverse consequences, and lead to the use of more expensive or less effective drugs, in contrast to patients who had undergone a complete drug allergy workup. several guidelines and/or consensus documents on general or specific drug class induced dhr s are available to support the medical decision process. the use of standardized systematic approaches for the diagnosis and management of dhr s carries the potential to improve outcomes and should thus be disseminated and implemented. consequently, the i nternational c ollaboration in a sthma, a llergy and i mmunology (i caall ), formed by the e uropean a cademy of a llergy and c linical i mmunology ( eaaci ), the a merican a cademy of a llergy, a sthma and i mmunology ( aaaai ), the a merican c ollege of a llergy, a sthma and i mmunology ( acaai ), and the w orld a llergy o rganization ( wao ), has decided to issue an i nternational con sensus (icon) on drug allergy. the purpose of this document is to highlight the key messages that are common to many of the existing guidelines, while critically reviewing and commenting on any differences and deficiencies of evidence, thus providing a comprehensive reference document for the diagnosis and management of dhrs.

title: cerebral organoids: ethical issues and consciousness assessment
display_name: Cerebral organoids: ethical issues and consciousness assessment
abstract: organoids are three-dimensional biological structures grown in vitro from different kinds of stem cells that self-organise mimicking real organs with organ-specific cell types. recently, researchers have managed to produce human organoids which have structural and functional properties very similar to those of different organs, such as the retina, the intestines, the kidneys, the pancreas, the liver and the inner ear. organoids are considered a great resource for biomedical research, as they allow for a detailed study of the development and pathologies of human cells; they also make it possible to test new molecules on human tissue. furthermore, organoids have helped research take a step forward in the field of personalised medicine and transplants. however, some ethical issues have arisen concerning the origin of the cells that are used to produce organoids (ie, human embryos) and their properties. in particular, there are new, relevant and so-far overlooked ethical questions concerning cerebral organoids. scientists have created so-called mini-brains as developed as a few-months-old fetus, albeit smaller and with many structural and functional differences. however, cerebral organoids exhibit neural connections and electrical activity, raising the question whether they are or (which is more likely) will one day be somewhat sentient. in principle, this can be measured with some techniques that are already available (the perturbational complexity index, a metric that is directly inspired by the main postulate of the integrated information theory of consciousness), which are used for brain-injured non-communicating patients. if brain organoids were to show a glimpse of sensibility, an ethical discussion on their use in clinical research and practice would be necessary.

title: bacteriocins from lactobacillus plantarum production, genetic organization and mode of action: produ o, organiza o gen tica e modo de a o
display_name: Bacteriocins from Lactobacillus plantarum production, genetic organization and mode of action: produção, organização genética e modo de ação
abstract: bacteriocins are biologically active proteins or protein complexes that display a bactericidal mode of action towards usually closely related species. numerous strains of bacteriocin producing lactobacillus plantarum have been isolated in the last two decades from different ecological niches including meat, fish, fruits, vegetables, and milk and cereal products. several of these plantaricins have been characterized and the aminoacid sequence determined. different aspects of the mode of action, fermentation optimization and genetic organization of the bacteriocin operon have been studied. however, numerous of bacteriocins produced by different lactobacillus plantarum strains have not been fully characterized. in this article, a brief overview of the classification, genetics, characterization, including mode of action and production optimization for bacteriocins from lactic acid bacteria in general, and where appropriate, with focus on bacteriocins produced by lactobacillus plantarum, is presented.

title: chatgpt: a revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
display_name: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
abstract: this study aims to examine the perspectives of various stakeholders, such as students and educators, on the use of artificial intelligence in teaching mathematics, specifically after the launch of chatgpt. the study adopts a qualitative case study approach consisting of two stages: content analysis of interviews and investigation of user experience. the first stage of the study shows that chatgpt is recognized for its improved math capabilities and ability to increase educational success by providing users with basic knowledge of mathematics and various topics. chatgpt can offer comprehensive instruction and assistance in the study of geometry, and the public discourse on social media is generally positive, with enthusiasm for the use of chatgpt in teaching mathematics and educational settings. however, there are also voices that approach using chatgpt in educational settings with caution. in the second stage of the study, the investigation of user experiences through three educational scenarios revealed various issues. chatgpt lacks a deep understanding of geometry and cannot effectively correct misconceptions. the accuracy and effectiveness of chatgpt solutions may depend on the complexity of the equation, input data, and the instructions given to chatgpt. chatgpt is expected to become more efficient in resolving increasingly complex mathematical problems. the results of this investigation propose a number of avenues for research that ought to be explored in order to guarantee the secure and conscientious integration of chatbots, especially chatgpt, into mathematics education and learning.

title: host defense against viral infection involves interferon mediated down-regulation of sterol biosynthesis
display_name: Host Defense against Viral Infection Involves Interferon Mediated Down-Regulation of Sterol Biosynthesis

authorships.name: Peter E. Phelan
institutions: Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute

authorships.name: Timothy F. Osborne
institutions: Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute

authorships.name: Ana Angulo
institutions: Consorci Institut D'Investigacions Biomediques August Pi I Sunyer

abstract: little is known about the protective role of inflammatory processes in modulating lipid metabolism in infection. here we report an intimate link between the innate immune response to infection and regulation of the sterol metabolic network characterized by down-regulation of sterol biosynthesis by an interferon regulatory loop mechanism. in time-series experiments profiling genome-wide lipid-associated gene expression of macrophages, we show a selective and coordinated negative regulation of the complete sterol pathway upon viral infection or cytokine treatment with ifn or but not tnf, il1 , or il6. quantitative analysis at the protein level of selected sterol metabolic enzymes upon infection shows a similar level of suppression. experimental testing of sterol metabolite levels using lipidomic-based measurements shows a reduction in metabolic output. on the basis of pharmacologic and rnai inhibition of the sterol pathway we show augmented protection against viral infection, and in combination with metabolite rescue experiments, we identify the requirement of the mevalonate-isoprenoid branch of the sterol metabolic network in the protective response upon statin or ifn treatment. conditioned media experiments from infected cells support an involvement of secreted type 1 interferon(s) to be sufficient for reducing the sterol pathway upon infection. moreover, we show that infection of primary macrophages containing a genetic knockout of the major type i interferon, ifn , leads to only a partial suppression of the sterol pathway, while genetic knockout of the receptor for all type i interferon family members, ifnar1, or associated signaling component, tyk2, completely abolishes the reduction of the sterol biosynthetic activity upon infection. levels of the proteolytically cleaved nuclear forms of srebp2, a key transcriptional regulator of sterol biosynthesis, are reduced upon infection and ifn treatment at both the protein and de novo transcription level. the reduction in srebf2 gene transcription upon infection and ifn treatment is also found to be strictly dependent on ifnar1. altogether these results show that type 1 ifn signaling is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the sterol metabolic network activity upon infection, thereby linking the regulation of the sterol pathway with interferon anti-viral defense responses. these findings bring a new link between sterol metabolism and interferon antiviral response and support the idea of using host metabolic modifiers of innate immunity as a potential antiviral strategy.

title: antibacterial immune competence of honey bees (apis mellifera) is adapted to different life stages and environmental risks
display_name: Antibacterial Immune Competence of Honey Bees (Apis mellifera) Is Adapted to Different Life Stages and Environmental Risks
abstract: the development of all honey bee castes proceeds through three different life stages all of which encounter microbial infections to a various extent. we have examined the immune strength of honey bees across all developmental stages with emphasis on the temporal expression of cellular and humoral immune responses upon artificial challenge with viable escherichia coli bacteria. we employed a broad array of methods to investigate defence strategies of infected individuals: (a) fate of bacteria in the haemocoel; (b) nodule formation and (c) induction of antimicrobial peptides (amps). newly emerged adult worker bees and drones were able to activate efficiently all examined immune reactions. the number of viable bacteria circulating in the haemocoel of infected bees declined rapidly by more than two orders of magnitude within the first 4-6 h post-injection (p.i.), coinciding with the occurrence of melanised nodules. antimicrobial activity, on the other hand, became detectable only after the initial bacterial clearance. these two temporal patterns of defence reactions very likely represent the constitutive cellular and the induced humoral immune response. a unique feature of honey bees is that a fraction of worker bees survives the winter season in a cluster mostly engaged in thermoregulation. we show here that the overall immune strength of winter bees matches that of young summer bees although nodulation reactions are not initiated at all. as expected, high doses of injected viable e.coli bacteria caused no mortality in larvae or adults of each age. however, drone and worker pupae succumbed to challenge with e.coli even at low doses, accompanied by a premature darkening of the pupal body. in contrast to larvae and adults, we observed no fast clearance of viable bacteria and no induction of amps but a rapid proliferation of e.coli bacteria in the haemocoel of bee pupae ultimately leading to their death.

title: reporting recommendations for tumor marker prognostic studies (remark): explanation and elaboration
display_name: Reporting Recommendations for Tumor Marker Prognostic Studies (REMARK): Explanation and Elaboration
abstract: the remark (reporting recommendations for tumor marker prognostic studies) guideline includes a checklist which aims to improve the reporting of these types of studies. here, we expand on the remark checklist to enhance its use and effectiveness through better understanding of the intent of each item and why the information is important to report. each checklist item of the remark guideline is explained in detail and accompanied by published examples of good reporting. the paper provides a comprehensive overview to educate on good reporting and provide a valuable reference of issues to consider when designing, conducting, and analyzing tumor marker studies and prognostic studies in medicine in general.

title: autoantibody epitope spreading in the pre-clinical phase predicts progression to rheumatoid arthritis
display_name: Autoantibody Epitope Spreading in the Pre-Clinical Phase Predicts Progression to Rheumatoid Arthritis

abstract: rheumatoid arthritis (ra) is a prototypical autoimmune arthritis affecting nearly 1% of the world population and is a significant cause of worldwide disability. though prior studies have demonstrated the appearance of ra-related autoantibodies years before the onset of clinical ra, the pattern of immunologic events preceding the development of ra remains unclear. to characterize the evolution of the autoantibody response in the preclinical phase of ra, we used a novel multiplex autoantigen array to evaluate development of the anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (acpa) and to determine if epitope spread correlates with rise in serum cytokines and imminent onset of clinical ra. to do so, we utilized a cohort of 81 patients with clinical ra for whom stored serum was available from 1-12 years prior to disease onset. we evaluated the accumulation of acpa subtypes over time and correlated this accumulation with elevations in serum cytokines. we then used logistic regression to identify a profile of biomarkers which predicts the imminent onset of clinical ra (defined as within 2 years of testing). we observed a time-dependent expansion of acpa specificity with the number of acpa subtypes. at the earliest timepoints, we found autoantibodies targeting several innate immune ligands including citrullinated histones, fibrinogen, and biglycan, thus providing insights into the earliest autoantigen targets and potential mechanisms underlying the onset and development of autoimmunity in ra. additionally, expansion of the acpa response strongly predicted elevations in many inflammatory cytokines including tnf- , il-6, il-12p70, and ifn- . thus, we observe that the preclinical phase of ra is characterized by an accumulation of multiple autoantibody specificities reflecting the process of epitope spread. epitope expansion is closely correlated with the appearance of preclinical inflammation, and we identify a biomarker profile including autoantibodies and cytokines which predicts the imminent onset of clinical arthritis.

title: a logical model provides insights into t cell receptor signaling
display_name: A Logical Model Provides Insights into T Cell Receptor Signaling

authorships.name: Julio Sáez-Rodríguez
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems

authorships.name: Rebecca Hemenway
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems

authorships.name: Ernst D Gilles
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems

authorships.name: Steffen Klamt
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Dynamics of Complex Technical Systems

abstract: cellular decisions are determined by complex molecular interaction networks. large-scale signaling networks are currently being reconstructed, but the kinetic parameters and quantitative data that would allow for dynamic modeling are still scarce. therefore, computational studies based upon the structure of these networks are of great interest. here, a methodology relying on a logical formalism is applied to the functional analysis of the complex signaling network governing the activation of t cells via the t cell receptor, the cd4/cd8 co-receptors, and the accessory signaling receptor cd28. our large-scale boolean model, which comprises 94 nodes and 123 interactions and is based upon well-established qualitative knowledge from primary t cells, reveals important structural features (e.g., feedback loops and network-wide dependencies) and recapitulates the global behavior of this network for an array of published data on t cell activation in wild-type and knock-out conditions. more importantly, the model predicted unexpected signaling events after antibody-mediated perturbation of cd28 and after genetic knockout of the kinase fyn that were subsequently experimentally validated. finally, we show that the logical model reveals key elements and potential failure modes in network functioning and provides candidates for missing links. in summary, our large-scale logical model for t cell activation proved to be a promising in silico tool, and it inspires immunologists to ask new questions. we think that it holds valuable potential in foreseeing the effects of drugs and network modifications.

title: lessons from first generation biofuels and implications for the sustainability appraisal of second generation biofuels
display_name: Lessons from first generation biofuels and implications for the sustainability appraisal of second generation biofuels
abstract: key lessons arising from 1g are potentially relevant to the sustainability appraisal of 2g biofuels depending on the particular circumstances or conditions under which 2g is introduced. we conclude that sustainability challenges commonly categorised as either economic, environmental or social are, in reality, more complexly interconnected (so that an artificial separation of these categories is problematic).
classification_path: Natural Science > Computer and Information Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning > Supervised Learning

title: atopic dermatitis
display_name: Atopic Dermatitis
abstract: atopic dermatitis (ad) is a chronic and relapsing disease affecting an increasing number of patients. usually starting in early childhood, ad can be the initial step of the so-called atopic march, i.e. followed by allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma. ad is a paradigmatic genetically complex disease involving gene-gene and gene-environment interactions. genetic linkage analysis as well as association studies have identified several candidate genes linked to either the epidermal barrier function or to the immune system. stress, bacterial or viral infections, the exposure to aero- or food-allergens as well as hygienic factors are discussed to aggravate symptoms of ad. athough generalized th2-deviated immune response is closely linked to the condition of ad, the skin disease itself is a biphasic inflammation with an initial th2 phase and while chronic lesions harbour th0/th1 cells. regulatory t cells have been shown to be altered in ad as well as the innate immune system in the skin. the main treatment-goals include the elimination of inflammation and infection, preserving and restoring the barrier function and controlling exacerbating factors. the overall future strategy in ad will be aimed to control skin inflammation by a more proactive management in order to potentially prevent the emergence of sensitization as well as to design customized management based on genetic and pathophysiologic information.
classification_path: Natural Science > Computer and Information Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning > Supervised Learning

title: bovine host genetic variation influences rumen microbial methane production with best selection criterion for low methane emitting and efficiently feed converting hosts based on metagenomic gene abundance
display_name: Bovine Host Genetic Variation Influences Rumen Microbial Methane Production with Best Selection Criterion for Low Methane Emitting and Efficiently Feed Converting Hosts Based on Metagenomic Gene Abundance
abstract: methane produced by methanogenic archaea in ruminants contributes significantly to anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. the host genetic link controlling microbial methane production is unknown and appropriate genetic selection strategies are not developed. we used sire progeny group differences to estimate the host genetic influence on rumen microbial methane production in a factorial experiment consisting of crossbred breed types and diets. rumen metagenomic profiling was undertaken to investigate links between microbial genes and methane emissions or feed conversion efficiency. sire progeny groups differed significantly in their methane emissions measured in respiration chambers. ranking of the sire progeny groups based on methane emissions or relative archaeal abundance was consistent overall and within diet, suggesting that archaeal abundance in ruminal digesta is under host genetic control and can be used to genetically select animals without measuring methane directly. in the metagenomic analysis of rumen contents, we identified 3970 microbial genes of which 20 and 49 genes were significantly associated with methane emissions and feed conversion efficiency respectively. these explained 81% and 86% of the respective variation and were clustered in distinct functional gene networks. methanogenesis genes (e.g. mcra and fmdb) were associated with methane emissions, whilst host-microbiome cross talk genes (e.g. tsta3 and fuci) were associated with feed conversion efficiency. these results strengthen the idea that the host animal controls its own microbiota to a significant extent and open up the implementation of effective breeding strategies using rumen microbial gene abundance as a predictor for difficult-to-measure traits on a large number of hosts. generally, the results provide a proof of principle to use the relative abundance of microbial genes in the gastrointestinal tract of different species to predict their influence on traits e.g. human metabolism, health and behaviour, as well as to understand the genetic link between host and microbiome.
classification_path: Natural Science > Computer and Information Science > Artificial Intelligence > Machine Learning > Supervised Learning

title: multisource neighborhood immune detector adaptive model for anomaly detection
display_name: Multisource Neighborhood Immune Detector Adaptive Model for Anomaly Detection

authorships.name: Liang Xi
institutions: Harbin University of Science and Technology

authorships.name: Ruidong Wang
institutions: Harbin University of Science and Technology

authorships.name: Fengbin Zhang
institutions: Harbin University of Science and Technology

abstract: the artificial immune system (ais) is one of the important branches of artificial intelligence technology, and it is widely used in many fields. the detector set is the core knowledge set, and the ais application effects are mainly determined by the generation, evolution, and detection of the detectors. presently, the problem space (shape-space) of ais mainly applied real-valued representation. but the real-valued detectors have some problems that have not been solved well, such as slow convergence speed of generation, holes in the nonself region, detector overlapping redundancy, dimension curse, etc., which lead to the unsatisfactory detection effects. moreover, artificial immune anomaly detection is a dynamic adaptive model, needs to be evolved adaptively with the detection environments. without better adaptive modeling, these problems mentioned before will get worse. in view of this, this article proposes a multisource immune detector adaptive model in neighborhood shape-space and applies it to anomaly detection: based on random, chaotic map and dna genetic algorithm (dna-ga), multisource neighborhood negative selection algorithm (msnnsa), multisource neighborhood immune detector generation algorithm (ms-nidga), and neighborhood immune anomaly detection algorithm (niada) are proposed, so that the generation and detection of immune detectors can be improved efficiently; introducing immune adaptive and feedback mechanism, multisource neighborhood immune detector adaptive model (ms-nidam) is built, so that the detectors can be adaptively evolved in a more targeted search domain, and keep better distribution to the nonself region in real time, so as to solve various problems existing in the real-valued shape-space under dynamic environment mentioned before and improve the overall detection performances. the experimental results show that ms-nidam can improve the detector generation/evolution efficiency, keep the up-to-date understanding of the changing environment, so as to obtain better overall detection performances and stability than other comparative methods.

title: application of clonal selection algorithm for pid controller synthesis of mimo systems in oil and gas industry
display_name: APPLICATION OF CLONAL SELECTION ALGORITHM FOR PID CONTROLLER SYNTHESIS OF MIMO SYSTEMS IN OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY
abstract: this paper presents the results of the smart technologies application to the synthesis of mimo-systems in oil and gas industry. in particular, there is considered a multidimensional multiply connected system for gas distillation process control through a distillation column with regulators configured on the basis of smart-technologies clonal selection algorithm (clonalg) of an artificial immune system (ais).
